principles.name: Employees
principles.description: People come first. High performers bring their real selves to work, speak up with respect, and keep raising their game.
evidence_signals: Helped a teammate grow or get through a hard stretch, with a visible result
Protected the team's wellbeing while still meeting a commitment
Spoke up respectfully about a problem instead of staying quiet

principles.name: Customer Service
principles.description: Deliver real value to customers and care about their success. Aim for the highest customer and user satisfaction.
evidence_signals: Names a specific customer or user and their problem
Owned a customer-impacting issue from first report to fix
Measures success by the customer's outcome, not only by shipping

principles.name: Innovation
principles.description: Innovate quickly in a competitive market, make it safe to experiment and take risks, and invest in value that lasts and scales.
evidence_signals: Proposed or tried a new approach and others adopted it
Ran a small experiment to test an idea before a big bet
Balances a new idea against long-term maintainability

principles.name: Integrity
principles.description: Build a lasting culture of honesty. Earn trust through clear expectations, accountability, measured results and ownership of outcomes.
evidence_signals: Delivered bad news early and honestly, with a plan
Refused to cut a corner on quality, security or data handling
Owns a mistake without blaming others and follows through on commitments

principles.name: Fun
principles.description: Work should be enjoyable. Inspire, win and celebrate together in ways that build lasting relationships.
evidence_signals: Gives a specific, sincere example of enjoying work with a team
Started a ritual or habit that made a team closer or happier

principles.name: Profitability
principles.description: Profit matters but is not the reason the company exists. Good values, smart choices and careful spending lead to it.
evidence_signals: Connects a technical or product decision to cost or business value
Chose a simpler or cheaper option when it served the customer equally well

principles.name: Inclusion and belonging (VIBE)
principles.description: Workday's VIBE program (Value Inclusion and Belonging for Everyone): a workplace where everyone can contribute their best and has fair opportunity.
evidence_signals: Made a team process more inclusive and describes the observed effect
Worked well with someone very different and explains the practices that helped

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, motivation, product area interest (platform, HCM, financials) and logistics. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Coding assessment or technical phone screen
rounds.notes: Some candidates report an online assessment (about three medium problems in two hours); others a live screen with one or two problems or an object-oriented design task. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Coding and object-oriented design
rounds.notes: One or two onsite rounds: algorithms plus modeling a domain with classes and interfaces. Java fluency helps. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: Mainly for senior levels. Enterprise-scale problems: multi-tenancy, tenant isolation, effective-dated data, audit, privacy and reliability.

rounds.name: Technical deep dive
rounds.notes: Defend decisions from a past project under scrutiny and say what you would change. Some guides combine it with behavioral questions.

rounds.name: Behavioral and values
rounds.interviewer_role: Engineer or manager from the team
rounds.notes: STAR stories mapped to the core values. Some candidates report questions on VIBE (inclusion and belonging).

rounds.name: Hiring manager and team match
rounds.notes: Scope, past projects, customer focus and team fit. Some loops end with a short executive or skip-level conversation.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Why Workday and enterprise HR or finance software. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: Product philosophy, how you discover and define customer problems, and one product you ran end to end.

rounds.name: Product case or design session
rounds.notes: A product design or strategy prompt for an enterprise product area. Some candidates report a take-home and a presentation instead.

rounds.name: Cross-functional interviews
rounds.notes: Several short interviews on working with engineering, design, sales and customers, plus values questions.

rounds.name: Executive interview
rounds.notes: Vision, market view and how you measure product success.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Match modeling background to a team. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical screen
rounds.notes: Hands-on SQL or pandas on messy data, plus statistics. ML engineer roles may get data structures questions. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: ML technical deep dive
rounds.notes: Model choice, features, evaluation metrics, serving, and fairness for HR and finance data.

rounds.name: Project presentation
rounds.notes: Walk through one past project: framing, data, model, deployment and outcome.

rounds.name: Hiring manager and culture fit
rounds.notes: Scope and level, stakeholder trust, and judgment when a model is right on paper but wrong in practice.

question_patterns.theme: Going the extra mile for a customer
question_patterns.pattern: A time the candidate went beyond the requirement to solve a customer's or user's real problem
A time the candidate helped a teammate grow, recover or succeed, and what changed for that person
Delivering bad news to a stakeholder, or refusing to cut a corner on quality, security or data
A new approach or improvement the candidate proposed, tested and got others to adopt
A disagreement with a teammate or product partner about an approach and how it was settled
Concrete changes the candidate made to make a team more inclusive or enjoyable, and the effect
A launch, project or model that did not go as planned and what the candidate does differently now

question_patterns.theme: Project the candidate ran end to end
question_patterns.pattern: Walk through one project: the customer problem, own role, what was cut and why, and the result
Why Workday, which product area, and how the candidate feels about regulated, slower-moving enterprise customers
Design an HR or finance system for many customer tenants with isolation, correctness, audit and burst load
Design configurable business rules, approval workflows or role-based access for sensitive people data

question_patterns.theme: ML on people and finance data
question_patterns.pattern: Build and evaluate a model on HR or finance data, including bias, interpretability and how stakeholders use it
Prioritize or design a feature for an enterprise HR or finance product, balancing customer configurability and simplicity, with a success metric

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you went beyond what was asked to help a customer or user.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name the customer and the real problem behind the request. Show why the stated requirement was not enough, what the candidate did personally, and how they checked the customer was better off (a metric, a renewal, direct feedback). Mention any trade-off with other work and how it was agreed. Pitfalls: a story with no real customer, or extra work nobody needed.

looking_for: Whether you care about the customer's outcome, not just the ticket
How you check the result with the customer
strong_signals: Names a specific customer and their pain
Shows what you did personally
Measures the outcome for the customer
watch_outs: No real customer in the story

sample_questions.question: Describe a customer-impacting problem you handled from start to finish.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Set the stakes: who was affected and how badly. Walk through detection, triage, communication with the customer or support team, the fix, and the follow-up that stopped it happening again. Show calm, clear updates and ownership even for parts outside the candidate's code. Pitfalls: stopping at the hotfix, or blaming another team.

looking_for: How dependable you are when customers are hurting
Whether you fix the cause, not only the symptom
strong_signals: Clear timeline from detection to follow-up
Keeps the customer and support informed
Adds a lasting fix or guardrail

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you supported a teammate who was struggling.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe what the candidate noticed and how they offered help without taking over. Show concrete actions (pairing, reshaping work, a frank but kind conversation) and the result for the teammate and the team. A strong answer shows care and still meets the team's commitments. Pitfalls: a story that is really about the candidate's own heroics.

looking_for: Whether you look after the people around you
How you help without taking over
strong_signals: Concrete actions such as pairing or reshaping work
Teammate is visibly better off afterwards
Team commitments are still met
watch_outs: The story is about your own heroics

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to deliver bad news to a stakeholder.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain the bad news (a slip, a defect, a missed target) and why it had to be said. Show the candidate raised it early, gave the facts without spin, took their share of responsibility, and came with options and a recovery plan. End with how trust held or grew. Pitfalls: waiting until the last moment, or softening the message until it misleads.

looking_for: Whether you are honest when it is uncomfortable
How you keep trust after bad news
strong_signals: Raises the issue early with plain facts
Brings options and a recovery plan
Owns your part
watch_outs: Softening the message until it misleads

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you made a difficult ethical choice at work.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the pressure (a deadline, a request to skip a check, to share data, or to hide a problem) and what was at stake. Show how the candidate decided, who they involved, and how they held the line respectfully while still helping the team move. Tie it to trust with customers whose people and money data Workday holds. Pitfalls: a dilemma with no real cost, or self-righteous framing.

looking_for: How you act when the right choice has a cost
Whether you protect customer data and trust
strong_signals: Explains the real pressure and stakes
Involves the right people and holds the line respectfully
Finds a way for the team to keep moving
watch_outs: A dilemma with no real cost

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a creative solution you proposed for a hard problem.
sample_questions.strong_answer: State the problem and why the usual approach failed. Explain the idea, how the candidate tested it cheaply before committing, and how they won support. Give the result and whether it was adopted beyond the original team. Note any long-term cost of the new approach. Pitfalls: novelty for its own sake, or an idea that never shipped.

looking_for: How you find new approaches to hard problems
Whether your ideas ship and get adopted
strong_signals: Tests the idea cheaply before committing
Wins support from others
Shows adoption and lasting value

sample_questions.question: What makes work enjoyable for you, and how do you make it enjoyable for others?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Answer sincerely with specifics: the kind of problems and people that energize the candidate, and one example of something they started (a demo day, a team ritual, celebrating a launch) and how the team responded. Keep it warm and genuine. Pitfalls: a stiff or rehearsed answer, or treating the question as unimportant.

looking_for: Whether you add warmth and energy to a team
How genuine you are
strong_signals: A specific example you started
Shows how the team responded

sample_questions.question: How have you made a team or process more inclusive?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name a concrete change, such as meeting formats that let quieter people contribute, clearer review criteria, or better onboarding, and why it was needed. Show what the candidate did and the observed effect (more voices in decisions, faster ramp-up, better retention). Pitfalls: only stating beliefs or intentions with no actions or results.

looking_for: Whether you take concrete steps toward inclusion
What changed because of them
strong_signals: Names a specific change to how the team works
Describes an observed effect

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to balance technical debt against delivering features.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the debt and its real cost (incidents, slow delivery, customer risk). Show how the candidate quantified it, made the case to product partners, and agreed a plan, for example a fixed share of each sprint or paying debt down inside related features. Give the outcome. Strong answers tie the choice to customers and cost. Pitfalls: all-or-nothing positions, or no data.

looking_for: How you weigh long-term health against short-term delivery
Whether you can make the case with data
strong_signals: Quantifies the cost of the debt
Agrees a plan with product partners
Ties the choice to customers and cost

sample_questions.question: Walk me through a product you ran end to end. What did you cut, and why?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start with the customer problem and how it was discovered (research, customer calls, data). Explain the candidate's role, the key decisions, and what was cut to ship, with the reasoning. Give measurable results for customers and the business, and what they would change. Match scope to the target level. Pitfalls: a feature list with no customer problem, or no hard choices.

looking_for: How you discover and define customer problems
What you cut and why
strong_signals: Starts from a real customer problem
Explains hard trade-offs and your own role
Measures customer and business results
watch_outs: A feature list with no problem behind it

sample_questions.question: Why Workday, and what draws you to enterprise HR and finance software?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Be specific: name a product area (HCM, financials, the platform, AI features) and link it to the candidate's past work and goals. Show an understanding of enterprise customers: configurability, compliance, long release cycles and high trust. Mention the people-first culture only with a concrete reason. Pitfalls: generic praise, or showing no interest in enterprise customers.

looking_for: Whether you understand what Workday builds and for whom
Which product area you want and why
strong_signals: Names a product area and links it to your experience
Shows you understand enterprise customers

sample_questions.question: Design a payroll processing system that runs for thousands of customer companies on a regular schedule.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify scale, pay frequencies and correctness needs. Snapshot effective-dated inputs per pay period and treat each calculation as a deterministic function of inputs and versioned rules. Fan out per-employee work with per-tenant concurrency limits so one large customer cannot slow others. Keep calculation traces for audit, handle retroactive changes with scoped recalculation, make disbursement idempotent, and resume from checkpoints so a few exceptions do not block everyone. Close with tenant-scoped privacy. Pitfalls: ignoring retro changes or audit.

looking_for: Whether you design for correctness and audit first
How you isolate tenants under burst load
strong_signals: Deterministic calculation from effective-dated inputs
Per-tenant limits and checkpointed retries
Idempotent payments and retained calculation traces
watch_outs: No audit trail or tenant isolation

sample_questions.question: Design an audit log that records every field change on employee and finance records for compliance.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify which records, retention, and who may read the log. Capture changes as append-only events with who, what, when, old and new values, and the business process that caused them. Partition by tenant, make the log tamper-evident, and keep it off the hot write path with a durable queue. Support as-of queries and exports for auditors, with access controls and data residency per customer. Discuss storage cost and deletion rules such as privacy requests. Pitfalls: mutable logs, or one shared store with no tenant boundary.

looking_for: How you meet compliance needs at scale
Whether you keep tenants and access separate
strong_signals: Append-only, tamper-evident events
Partitioned by tenant with residency rules
Handles retention and privacy deletion
watch_outs: No tenant boundary or access control

sample_questions.question: How would you implement role-based access control for sensitive HR data across many customers?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the roles and data types (pay, health, performance). Model permissions per tenant with roles, security groups and scopes such as a manager's subtree in the org hierarchy, with effective dates. Enforce checks in one service close to the data, cache decisions carefully, and log every access to sensitive fields. Allow per-customer configuration within safe limits, and test that one tenant can never see another's data. Pitfalls: checks only in the UI, or ignoring org changes over time.

looking_for: How you protect sensitive people data
Whether you handle hierarchy and change over time
strong_signals: Scopes access by org subtree with effective dates
Enforces checks near the data and logs access
Keeps per-customer configuration within safe limits
watch_outs: Access checks only in the UI

sample_questions.question: How would you build a model to predict employee attrition, and how would you check it for bias?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define the target (voluntary leave within a window) and the decision it supports. Pick features carefully, excluding protected attributes and close proxies, and watch for leakage. Start with an interpretable baseline, then a stronger model, and evaluate with metrics that fit class imbalance. Measure performance and error rates across groups, explain predictions to HR users, and keep a human in the loop. Pitfalls: using sensitive data blindly, or reporting accuracy alone.

looking_for: How you frame an ML problem on people data
Whether you take fairness and interpretability seriously
strong_signals: Clear target and the decision it supports
Checks leakage, imbalance and group-level errors
Keeps a human in the loop

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time your analysis contradicted what the business believed.
sample_questions.strong_answer: State the belief, what the data showed, and how the candidate checked their own work first. Show how they presented it: plain language, the business impact, and a recommendation, with respect for the people who held the belief. Give the outcome and how trust in the analysis grew. Pitfalls: proving people wrong as the goal, or giving up when challenged.

looking_for: Whether you speak up honestly with data
How you build trust with business partners
strong_signals: Double-checks the analysis first
Explains impact in plain language with a recommendation
Keeps the relationship intact
watch_outs: Proving people wrong as the goal

sample_questions.question: How would you prioritize features for a new employee onboarding module?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the customer (company size, industry) and users: new hires, managers, HR admins. Map the onboarding journey and the main pains (paperwork, slow access to tools, unclear first weeks). List options, prioritize by customer value, effort and fit with existing HCM data, and recommend a first release. Define success metrics such as time to productivity and admin hours saved, with guardrails like data accuracy. Pitfalls: designing for one user only, or no metric.

looking_for: Whether you consider every user of an enterprise product
How you prioritize and pick a first release
strong_signals: Separates new hires, managers and HR admins
Prioritizes by value, effort and platform fit
Defines success and guardrail metrics

sample_questions.question: How would you balance enterprise customers' demand for customization with keeping the product simple?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Frame the tension: large customers want their own processes, but each option adds cost, test burden and confusion. Segment requests by how many customers need them and the value at stake. Propose layers: good defaults, a small set of supported configuration points, and an extension platform for the rest. Explain how to decide when a request becomes a core feature, and how to measure success (adoption, support load, upgrade pain). Pitfalls: saying yes to every big customer, or refusing all customization.

looking_for: How you handle the pull between customization and simplicity
Whether you have a clear rule for what goes into the core
strong_signals: Segments requests by reach and value
Proposes defaults, configuration points and extensions
Measures adoption, support load and upgrade pain
watch_outs: Saying yes to every large customer

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Software Engineer I. Delivers well-defined tasks with guidance; loop focuses on coding and behavioral rounds.
Software Engineer II. Delivers features within a team with growing independence.
Software Engineer III. Owns features end to end and handles some ambiguity; may get a design round.
Senior Software Engineer. Owns components or services, designs for multi-tenant scale, and mentors others.
Principal Software Engineer. Leads technical direction across teams; loop adds deeper design and leadership discussion.
Senior Principal Software Engineer. Shapes architecture for a product area or platform.
Owns a product area, its roadmap and metrics, and works across engineering, UX and go-to-market.
Sets strategy for a large product area and handles conflicting stakeholder needs across teams.
Owns models from framing to deployment and earns the trust of business stakeholders.

persona.tone: Warm, friendly and people-focused, with a professional enterprise feel
persona.pace: Moderate; lets the candidate tell a full story, then asks for specifics
persona.pushback_style: Asks for the customer impact, the candidate's own part, and what they would do differently; in design rounds asks about tenant isolation, correctness and audit
persona.closing_style: Leaves time for the candidate's questions about the team, culture and product area

case_style.notes: PM cases are enterprise product strategy and design: prioritizing features for HCM or finance products, customization versus simplicity, and success metrics. Some loops use a take-home with a presentation. Market sizing is rarely reported.

What is the Workday interview process like, round by round (Design Gurus)
Top Workday behavioral interview questions (Design Gurus)
What to expect in the Workday system design interview (Design Gurus)

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: the six core values come from Workday's official values page. 'Inclusion and belonging (VIBE)' is not a core value; it is Workday's inclusion program (now 'Value Inclusion and Belonging for Everyone'), added because prep guides and candidate reports mention VIBE questions. The claim that interviewers score against the values comes from prep sites, not Workday.

loop_structure: no official Workday interview guide was found. Rounds come from third-party prep sites that disagree on the order, the online assessment, the take-home and the executive close; the loop varies by team. PM and data_ml loops come mostly from one prep site (CleverPrep).

question_patterns: sample questions come from prep sites that aggregate candidate reports (CleverPrep, Design Gurus, techinterview.org); some may be the sites' own practice questions rather than verified Workday questions.

bar_by_level: P1 to P6 labels and SWE titles come from Levels.fyi and ScaleEngineer, not Workday; scope text is our summary. PM and data scientist titles are job titles from CleverPrep, not confirmed level codes.
persona: inferred from the values page and prep guides that stress a warm, people-first register; no source describes interviewer style directly.
scoring_weights: our estimate from the values emphasis (Employees, Customer Service, Integrity) and enterprise design themes; no public source gives weights.
case_style: based on PM question lists from one prep site and a few candidate reports of a design session or take-home; split between product sense and system thinking is our estimate.
